formulations.label: Film-coated tablets (perindopril arginine)
formulations.note: Doses are stated as perindopril arginine: 5 mg perindopril arginine contains 3.395 mg perindopril. The 5 mg tablet is scored and can be divided into equal doses.

src.q: One film-coated tablet contains 3.395 mg perindopril corresponding to 5 mg perindopril arginine.
The tablet can be divided into equal doses.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Hypertension; symptomatic heart failure; stable coronary artery disease (to reduce the risk of cardiac events after myocardial infarction and/or revascularisation).

src.q: Hypertension: Treatment of hypertension. Heart failure: Treatment of symptomatic heart failure.
Stable coronary artery disease: Reduction of risk of cardiac events in patients with a history of myocardial infarction and/or revascularisation.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only or shared-care restriction stated in the perindopril arginine SmPC. Dual RAAS blockade, if absolutely necessary, only under specialist supervision (see cautions).

items.t: Start 5 mg once daily in the morning; may increase to 10 mg once daily after one month. Strongly activated renin-angiotensin system (renovascular hypertension, salt/volume depletion, cardiac decompensation, severe hypertension): start 2.5 mg under medical supervision.

src.q: The recommended starting dose is 5 mg given once daily in the morning.
A starting dose of 2.5 mg is recommended in such patients and the initiation of treatment should take place under medical supervision.
The dose may be increased to 10 mg once daily after one month of treatment.

items.t: Already on a diuretic: stop the diuretic 2-3 days before if possible; if it cannot be stopped, start at 2.5 mg and monitor renal function and serum potassium.

src.q: If possible, the diuretic should be discontinued 2 to 3 days before beginning therapy with Coversyl Arginine
In hypertensive patients in whom the diuretic cannot be discontinued, therapy with Coversyl Arginine should be initiated with a 2.5 mg dose. Renal function and serum potassium should be monitored.

items.t: Start 2.5 mg in the morning under close medical supervision; may increase after 2 weeks to 5 mg once daily if tolerated. Monitor blood pressure, renal function and potassium closely before and during treatment.

src.q: be introduced under close medical supervision with a recommended starting dose of 2.5 mg taken in the morning. This dose may be increased after 2 weeks to 5 mg once daily if tolerated.
Blood pressure, renal function and serum potassium should be monitored closely, both before and during treatment with Coversyl Arginine

items.t: 5 mg once daily for two weeks, then 10 mg once daily if the 5 mg dose is well tolerated, depending on renal function.

src.q: Coversyl Arginine should be introduced at a dose of 5 mg once daily for two weeks, then increased to 10 mg once daily, depending on renal function and provided that the 5 mg dose is well tolerated.

items.t: Elderly: hypertension - start 2.5 mg, increase to 5 mg after one month, then 10 mg if needed depending on renal function. Stable coronary artery disease - 2.5 mg once daily for one week, then 5 mg the next week, then up to 10 mg depending on renal function.

src.q: In elderly patients, treatment should be initiated at a dose of 2.5 mg which may be progressively increased to 5 mg after one month then to 10 mg if necessary depending on renal function
Elderly patients should receive 2.5 mg once daily for one week, then 5 mg once daily the next week, before increasing the dose up to 10 mg once daily depending on renal function

items.t: Safety and efficacy below 18 years not established; no posology recommendation. Use in children and adolescents is not recommended.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of perindopril in children and adolescents aged below 18 years have not been established.
Therefore, use in children and adolescents is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to perindopril, any excipient or any other ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to any of the excipients or to any other ACE inhibitor

items.t: History of angioedema with previous ACE inhibitor therapy; hereditary or idiopathic angioedema.

src.q: History of angioedema associated with previous ACE inhibitor therapy
Hereditary or idiopathic angioedema

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy (see sections 4.4 and 4.6)

items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

src.q: Concomitant use of Coversyl Arginine with aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes mellitus or renal impairment (GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)

items.t: With sacubitril/valsartan; do not start perindopril within 36 hours of the last sacubitril/valsartan dose.

src.q: Concomitant use with sacubitril/valsartan therapy, Coversyl Arginine must not be initiated earlier than 36 hours after the last dose of sacubitril/valsartan

items.t: Extracorporeal treatments where blood contacts negatively charged surfaces (e.g. certain high-flux dialysis/haemofiltration membranes, LDL apheresis with dextran sulfate).

src.q: Extracorporeal treatments leading to contact of blood with negatively charged surfaces (see section 4.5)

items.t: Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a single functioning kidney.

src.q: Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a single functioning kidney

items.t: Symptomatic hypotension: more likely with volume depletion (diuretics, salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea, vomiting), severe renin-dependent hypertension or more severe heart failure. Monitor starting and dose changes closely in those at risk, including ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease.

src.q: more likely to occur in patients who have been volume-depleted e.g. by diuretic therapy, dietary salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea or vomiting, or who have severe renin-dependent hypertension
In patients at increased risk of symptomatic hypotension, initiation of therapy and dose adjustment should be closely monitored

items.t: Stable coronary artery disease: if unstable angina occurs in the first month, carefully reassess benefit and risk before continuing.

src.q: If an episode of unstable angina pectoris (major or not) occurs during the first month of perindopril treatment, a careful appraisal of the benefit/risk should be performed before treatment continuation.

items.t: Mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: give with caution.

src.q: should be given with caution to patients with mitral valve stenosis and obstruction in the outflow of the left ventricle such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.t: Renal impairment (CrCl below 60 mL/min): adjust the starting dose to creatinine clearance; monitor potassium and creatinine. Renal artery stenosis: urea and creatinine may rise; start under close supervision with low doses and careful titration.

src.q: In cases of renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 60 ml/min) the initial perindopril dosage should be adjusted according to the patient's creatinine clearance
In these patients, treatment should be started under close medical supervision with low doses and careful dose titration.

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal angioedema presenting as abdominal pain) can occur at any time. Stop promptly and monitor until resolved; airway involvement needs emergency treatment. Higher rate in black patients.

src.q: This may occur at any time during therapy . In such cases, Coversyl Arginine should promptly be discontinued and appropriate monitoring should be initiated and continued until complete resolution of symptoms has occurred.
Where there is involvement of the tongue, glottis or larynx, likely to cause airway obstruction, emergency therapy should be administered promptly.
Intestinal angioedema should be included in the differential diagnosis of patients on ACE inhibitors presenting with abdominal pain.
ACE inhibitors cause a higher rate of angioedema in black patients than in non-black patients.

items.t: History of angioedema not caused by an ACE inhibitor: may be at higher risk of angioedema on an ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Patients with a history of angioedema unrelated to ACE inhibitor therapy may be at increased risk of angioedema while receiving an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis: extreme caution in collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, allopurinol or procainamide, especially with renal impairment; check white cell counts periodically.

src.q: Perindopril should be used with extreme caution in patients with collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, treatment with allopurinol or procainamide
periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is advised

items.t: Hyperkalaemia risk with renal impairment, age over 70, diabetes, dehydration, acute cardiac decompensation, metabolic acidosis, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes, heparin, co-trimoxazole, aldosterone antagonists or ARBs. Use such combinations with caution and monitor potassium and renal function.

src.q: Risk factors for the development of hyperkalaemia include those with renal insufficiency, worsening of renal function, age (> 70 years), diabetes mellitus
in particular dehydration, acute cardiac decompensation, metabolic acidosis

or those patients taking other drugs associated with increases in serum potassium (e.g. heparin, co-trimoxazole also known as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole) and especially aldosterone antagonists or angiotensin-receptor blockers
Potassium-sparing diuretics and angiotensin-receptor blockers should be used with caution in patients receiving ACE inhibitors, and serum potassium and renal function should be monitored.

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor with ARB or aliskiren) not recommended; if absolutely necessary only under specialist supervision with close monitoring. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
ACE-inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Diabetes on insulin or oral antidiabetics: monitor glycaemic control closely in the first month.

src.q: glycaemic control should be closely monitored during the first month of treatment with an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Hepatic failure (rare): stop if jaundice or marked rise in liver enzymes.

src.q: Patients receiving ACE inhibitors who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue the ACE inhibitor and receive appropriate medical follow-up

items.t: Major surgery or anaesthesia: stop perindopril one day before surgery; correct hypotension with volume expansion.

src.q: The treatment should be discontinued one day prior to the surgery.
If hypotension occurs and is considered to be due to this mechanism, it can be corrected by volume expansion.

items.t: Primary hyperaldosteronism: generally will not respond; not recommended.

src.q: Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism generally will not respond to anti-hypertensive drugs acting through inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system. Therefore, the use of this product is not recommended.

items.t: Lithium and potassium-raising combinations generally not recommended (see interactions).

src.q: The combination of lithium and perindopril is generally not recommended
The combination of perindopril and potassium-sparing drugs, potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes is generally not recommended

items.t: Persistent dry cough can occur and resolves after stopping.

src.q: Characteristically, the cough is non-productive, persistent and resolves after discontinuation of therapy.

items.t: Anaphylactoid reactions with high-flux dialysis membranes, LDL apheresis with dextran sulfate, and desensitisation (e.g. hymenoptera venom); withhold the ACE inhibitor before each apheresis or desensitisation.

src.q: Anaphylactoid reactions have been reported in patients dialysed with high flux membranes, and treated concomitantly with an ACE inhibitor.
These reactions were avoided by temporarily withholding ACE inhibitor therapy prior to each apheresis.

items.t: Recent kidney transplant: no experience.

src.q: There is no experience regarding the administration of Coversyl Arginine in patients with a recent kidney transplantation.

items.t: Contains lactose: patients with rare hereditary galactose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or total lactase deficiency should not take it.

src.q: Due to the presence of lactose, patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption, or total lactase deficiency should not take this medicinal product.

items.t: Aliskiren, potassium salts, potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, amiloride), other ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, heparins, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole: increased risk of hyperkalaemia. Combination not recommended; if needed, use with caution and monitor potassium frequently.

src.q: Some drugs or therapeutic classes may increase the occurrence of hyperkalaemia: aliskiren, potassium salts, potassium-sparing diuretics

potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, triamterene or amiloride), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-II receptors antagonists, NSAIDs, heparins, immunosuppressant agents such as ciclosporin or tacrolimus, trimethoprim and cotrimoxazole (trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole)

Therefore, the combination of Coversyl Arginine with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended. If concomitant use is indicated, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: Spironolactone or eplerenone in heart failure (12.5-50 mg/day with low-dose ACE inhibitor): risk of potentially lethal hyperkalaemia. Check for hyperkalaemia and renal impairment before starting; monitor potassium and creatinine weekly in the first month, then monthly. MHRA: use with caution, lowest effective doses, regular potassium and renal monitoring.

src.q: Before initiating the combination, check the absence of hyperkalaemia and renal impairment. A close monitoring of the kalaemia and creatininaemia is recommended in the first month of the treatment once a week at the beginning and, monthly thereafter.
concomitant use of spironolactone with ACEi or ARB increases the risk of severe hyperkalaemia, particularly in patients with marked renal impairment, and should be used with caution
With eplerenone or spironolactone at doses between 12.5 mg to 50 mg by day and with low doses of ACE inhibitors
use the lowest effective doses of spironolactone and ACEi or ARB if coadministration is considered essential

items.t: NSAIDs (including aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses of 3 g/day or more, COX-2 inhibitors): reduced antihypertensive effect; risk of worsening renal function (possible acute renal failure) and raised potassium. Use with caution, especially in the elderly; keep hydrated and consider monitoring renal function.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE-inhibitors and NSAIDs may lead to an increased risk of worsening of renal function, including possible acute renal failure, and an increase in serum potassium

The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly. Patients should be adequately hydrated and consideration should be given to monitoring renal function after initiation of concomitant therapy, and periodically thereafter.
acetylsalicylic acid at anti-inflammatory dosage regimens, COX-2 inhibitors and non-selective NSAIDs

items.t: ARBs or aliskiren (dual RAAS blockade): more hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal failure. Not recommended (aliskiren is contraindicated with diabetes or renal impairment: see contraindications).

src.q: is associated with a higher frequency of adverse events such as hypotension, hyperkalaemia and decreased renal function (including acute renal failure) compared to the use of a single RAAS-acting agent
Combination use of medicines from two classes of RAS blocking agents (ACE-inhibitors, ARBs, or aliskiren) is not recommended.

items.t: Sacubitril/valsartan: contraindicated (angioedema); 36-hour gap either way. Racecadotril, mTOR inhibitors and gliptins (e.g. linagliptin, sitagliptin, vildagliptin): higher angioedema risk; take care when starting them in a patient already on an ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated as this increases the risk of angioedema

Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with racecadotril, mTOR inhibitors (e.g. sirolimus, everolimus, temsirolimus) and gliptins (e.g. linagliptin, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, vildagliptin) may lead to an increased risk for angioedema

items.t: Antidiabetic medicines (insulins, oral agents): greater glucose lowering with risk of hypoglycaemia, mostly in the first weeks and in renal impairment.

src.q: may cause an increased blood-glucose lowering effect with risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Non-potassium-sparing diuretics: excessive fall in blood pressure when perindopril is started; stop the diuretic or start low; monitor creatinine in the first weeks.

src.q: Patients on diuretics, and especially those who are volume and/or salt depleted, may experience excessive reduction in blood pressure after initiation of therapy with an ACE inhibitor.

The possibility of hypotensive effects can be reduced by discontinuation of the diuretic, by increasing volume or salt intake prior to initiating therapy with low and progressive doses of perindopril.
In all cases, renal function (creatinine levels) must be monitored during the first few weeks of ACE inhibitor therapy.

items.t: Other antihypertensives, nitrates and vasodilators, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, some anaesthetics: further fall in blood pressure. Sympathomimetics may reduce the antihypertensive effect.

src.q: Concomitant use with nitroglycerin and other nitrates, or other vasodilators, may further reduce blood pressure.
Concomitant use of certain anaesthetic medicinal products, tricyclic antidepressants and antipsychotics with ACE inhibitors may result in further reduction of blood pressure
Sympathomimetics may reduce the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors.

items.t: Lithium: not recommended; if needed, monitor lithium levels carefully. Baclofen: increased antihypertensive effect, monitor blood pressure. Estramustine: more angioedema. Injectable gold: rare nitritoid reactions.

src.q: Use of perindopril with lithium is not recommended, but if the combination proves necessary, careful monitoring of serum lithium levels should be performed
Baclofen: Increased antihypertensive effect. Monitor blood pressure and adapt antihypertensive dosage if necessary.
Estramustine: Risk of increased adverse effects such as angioneurotic oedema (angioedema).
Nitritoid reactions (symptoms include facial flushing, nausea, vomiting and hypotension) have been reported rarely in patients on therapy with injectable gold (sodium aurothiomalate)

items.t: Dose by creatinine clearance: 60 mL/min or more - 5 mg daily; above 30 and below 60 mL/min - 2.5 mg daily; above 15 and below 30 mL/min - 2.5 mg every other day; below 15 mL/min on haemodialysis - 2.5 mg on the day of dialysis, taken after dialysis.

src.q: Dosage in patients with renal impairment should be based on creatinine clearance as outlined in table 1 below
ClCR ≥ 60 5 mg per day 30 < ClCR < 60 2.5 mg per day 15 < ClCR < 30 2.5 mg every other day Haemodialysed patients * ClCR < 15 2.5 mg on the day of dialysis
For patients on haemodialysis, the dose should be taken after dialysis.

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

src.q: eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2
Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is:

items.t: SPS: some rise in creatinine is expected; a transient fall in renal function should not prompt stopping. Acceptable: creatinine rise under 50% above baseline (if below 266 micromol/L) or eGFR fall under 10% (if eGFR over 25 mL/min/1.73 m²). In CKD: eGFR fall under 25% or creatinine rise under 30% - do not change the dose; eGFR fall over 25% or creatinine rise over 30% - look for other causes (e.g. volume depletion, NSAIDs) and, if none, stop or reduce to the previously tolerated dose.

src.q: A transient decrease in renal function should not prompt stopping ACEI/ARB

An increase in serum creatinine of less than 50% above baseline, as long as it is less than 266 micromol/L, or a decrease in eGFR of less than 10% from baseline, as long as eGFR is over 25 mL/min/1.73 m2, can be considered as acceptable.
Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease eGFR decrease less than 25% or creatinine increase less than 30% from baseline Do not change dose
eGFR decrease more than 25%; creatinine increase more than 30% Investigate other causes of deteriorating renal function, such as volume depletion or concurrent medication such as, NSAIDs.
If no alternative cause is identified: Stop ACEI/ARB or reduce to previously tolerated dose

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in hepatic impairment (in cirrhosis, parent-drug clearance halves but perindoprilat formation is not reduced).

src.q: No dosage adjustment is necessary in patients with hepatic impairment
However, the quantity of perindoprilat formed is not reduced and therefore no dosage adjustment is required

items.t: Rarely ACE inhibitors cause cholestatic jaundice progressing to fulminant hepatic necrosis; stop if jaundice or marked liver enzyme rise.

src.q: Rarely, ACE inhibitors have been associated with a syndrome that starts with cholestatic jaundice and progresses to fulminant hepatic necrosis and (sometimes) death.

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in the first trimester; contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. Do not start in pregnancy; stop as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed and switch if appropriate. If exposed from the second trimester, ultrasound check of fetal renal function and skull; watch the newborn for hypotension.

src.q: The use of ACE inhibitors is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy
The use of ACE inhibitors is contra-indicated during the 2nd and 3rd trimester of pregnancy
ACE inhibitors should not be initiated during pregnancy.
When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with ACE inhibitors should be stopped immediately, and, if appropriate, alternative therapy should be started.
Should exposure to ACE inhibitor have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary. On diagnosis of pregnancy, stop as soon as possible.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby; use after about 20 weeks can cause problems in the baby. Extra monitoring of amniotic fluid and fetal growth is needed if continued after about 20 weeks.

src.q: Taking an ACE-I in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
Taking an ACE-I after around 20 weeks of pregnancy can cause a number of problems in your baby
If you continue to take an ACE-I after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.

items.t: SmPC: no information; not recommended. Alternatives with better established safety are preferable, especially with a newborn or preterm infant.

src.q: is not recommended and alternative treatments with better established safety profiles during breast-feeding are preferable, especially while nursing a newborn or preterm infant.

items.t: MHRA (2009): perindopril not recommended in breastfeeding; prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm baby. Clarification: not absolutely contraindicated; may be prescribed if essential for the mother.

src.q: ramipril, lisinopril, fosinopril, trandolapril, moexipril, or perindopril: use in breastfeeding is not recommended
they are not absolutely contraindicated. Healthcare professionals may prescribe these medicines during breastfeeding if they consider that this treatment is essential for the lactating mother.

items.t: SPS (2023): perindopril can be used with caution; enalapril is preferred. Very long half-life raises the risk of accumulation in the infant (not shown to date). Watch the infant for hypotension (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding, poor weight gain) and, in younger infants, for normal wet nappies.

src.q: Perindopril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril is preferred.
Perindopril has a very long half life (30 hours for perindopril and 120 hours for perindoprilat), which increases the risk of drug accumulation in the infant and side-effects.
monitor the infant for hypotension which may manifest as drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding and inadequate weight gain
In younger infants, monitor for normal urine production (wet nappies).

items.t: Planning pregnancy: switch to an antihypertensive with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ACE inhibitor treatment is essential. No effect on fertility reported.

src.q: Unless continued ACE inhibitor therapy is considered essential, patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative antihypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy.
Fertility: There was no effect on reproductive performance or fertility.

items.t: Common: dizziness, headache, paraesthesia, vertigo, visual disturbances, tinnitus, hypotension, cough, dyspnoea, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, taste disturbance, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, itching, rash, muscle cramps, asthenia.

src.q: The most frequent adverse events reported in clinical trials and observed with perindopril are: dizziness, headache, paraesthesia, vertigo, visual disturbances, tinnitus, hypotension, cough, dyspnoea
abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhoea, dysgeusia, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, rash, muscle cramps, and asthenia.

items.t: Angioedema (face, lips, tongue, glottis, larynx; also intestinal): can occur at any time. Stop the ACE inhibitor at once and do not restart. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema may not respond to adrenaline. Airway involvement needs emergency treatment.

src.q: if angioedema is suspected in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, discontinue the ACE inhibitor immediately and do not restart
bradykinin-mediated angioedema is unlikely to respond to standard anaphylaxis treatments including adrenaline (epinephrine)
Angioedema associated with laryngeal oedema may be fatal.

items.t: Uncommon: hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, renal insufficiency. Rare: acute renal failure, anuria/oliguria, SIADH.

src.q: Hypoglycaemia (see sections 4.4 and 4.5) Uncommon* Hyperkalaemia, reversible on discontinuation (see section 4.4) Uncommon* Hyponatraemia Uncommon*
Renal insufficiency Uncommon Acute renal failure Rare* Anuria/Oliguria Rare*
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) Rare

items.t: Very rare: agranulocytosis or pancytopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency; pancreatitis; hepatitis; erythema multiforme; myocardial infarction or stroke possibly from excessive hypotension in high-risk patients.

src.q: Agranulocytosis or pancytopenia Very rare
Leucopenia/neutropenia Very rare
Thrombocytopenia Very rare
Erythema multiforme Very rare
Stroke possibly secondary to excessive hypotension in high-risk patients (see section 4.4) Very rare
Haemolytic anaemia in patients with a congenital deficiency of G-6PDH (see section 4.4) Very rare
Pancreatitis Very rare Hepato-biliary Disorders Hepatitis either cytolytic or cholestatic (see section 4.4) Very rare
Myocardial infarction, possibly secondary to excessive hypotension in high risk patients (see section 4.4) Very rare

items.t: SPS baseline: blood pressure, eGFR or serum creatinine, serum potassium, serum sodium. Starting is not normally appropriate if potassium is above 5.0 mmol/L.

src.q: Baseline Blood pressure Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum potassium Serum sodium
Initiation not normally appropriate if pre-treatment potassium greater than 5.0mmol/L

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting in severe or unstable heart failure, renovascular disease, eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², sodium below 130 mmol/L, hypovolaemia, systolic BP below 90 mmHg, multiple or high-dose diuretics (equivalent to furosemide 80 mg daily or more), high-dose vasodilator, or haemodynamically significant valve disease.

src.q: Seek specialist advice prior to initiation for patients where there is: severe or unstable heart failure renovascular disease eGFR less than 30ml/min/1.73m2 hyponatraemia (sodium less than 130mmol/L) hypovolaemia hypotension (systolic blood pressure less than 90mmHg)
concomitant multiple or high-dose diuretics (equivalent to 80mg furosemide daily or more) concomitant high-dose vasodilator haemodynamically significant valve disease

items.t: SPS after starting or a dose change: heart failure - renal function, sodium and potassium within 1-2 weeks (5-7 days with other risk factors); hypertension - renal function, sodium, potassium within 1-2 weeks, BP within 1 month.

src.q: Heart failure with other risk factors Within 5 - 7 days
Hypertension Within 1 - 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Serum sodium Serum potassium Within 1 month Blood pressure

items.t: SPS once stable: heart failure every 3-6 months; hypertension annually. Repeat at any time if acutely unwell.

src.q: Ongoing once stable Heart failure Every 3 - 6 months
Hypertension Annually Serum sodium Serum potassium
Repeat monitoring at any time patient acutely unwell or their renal function may be compromised.

items.t: SPS abnormal results: potassium 6.0 mmol/L or above in CKD - stop the ACE inhibitor (after stopping other potassium-raising drugs) and seek specialist advice; sodium below 132 mmol/L - specialist advice.

src.q: Value 6.0 mmol/L or above in people with CKD Stop ACEI/ARB after stopping other drugs that may increase potassium and seek specialist advice.
Sodium Value is below 132mmol/L Obtain specialist advice

items.t: Stop if angioedema, jaundice or marked rise in liver enzymes.

src.q: Coversyl Arginine should promptly be discontinued
Patients receiving ACE inhibitors who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue the ACE inhibitor

items.t: Once daily in the morning before a meal (food reduces conversion to the active metabolite).

src.q: Coversyl Arginine is recommended to be taken once daily in the morning before a meal.
As ingestion of food decreases conversion to perindoprilat, hence bioavailability

items.t: Seek urgent help for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing, even after long use; do not take further doses.

src.q: seek urgent medical attention if you develop swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or experience difficulty breathing or swallowing whilst taking ACE inhibitors
do not take further doses of your ACE inhibitor if angioedema is suspected and inform a healthcare professional immediately

items.t: Planning pregnancy or pregnant: contact the doctor to switch medicine.

src.q: If you find out that you are pregnant whilst taking an ACE-I, you should contact your doctor as soon as possible so that you can be switched to another medicine.

items.t: Low blood pressure reactions (especially at the start) can affect driving or using machines.

src.q: As a result the ability to drive or operate machinery may be impaired.

items.t: Report any sign of infection (e.g. sore throat, fever).

src.q: patients should be instructed to report any sign of infection (e.g. sore throat, fever)

items.t: Avoid potassium salt substitutes unless advised (risk of high potassium).

src.q: The use of potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, or potassium-containing salt substitutes particularly in patients with impaired renal function may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.

rules.concern: Hypersensitivity to perindopril or any other ACE inhibitor (including previous ACE inhibitor angioedema)
rules.consequence: Hypersensitivity reaction / angioedema.
rules.action: Do not use.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to any of the excipients or to any other ACE inhibitor
History of angioedema associated with previous ACE inhibitor therapy

rules.consequence: Risk of angioedema.
rules.action: Do not use.

src.q: Hereditary or idiopathic angioedema

rules.concern: History of angioedema not caused by an ACE inhibitor
rules.consequence: May be at increased risk of angioedema while taking an ACE inhibitor.
rules.action: Be aware of the increased angioedema risk (hereditary or idiopathic angioedema, or angioedema with a previous ACE inhibitor, are contraindications).
rules.sourceWording: may be at increased risk of angioedema

src.q: Patients with a history of angioedema unrelated to ACE inhibitor therapy may be at increased risk of angioedema while receiving an ACE inhibitor

rules.concern: Significant bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis to a single functioning kidney
rules.consequence: Increased risk of severe hypotension and renal insufficiency.
